label: Atlantic
description: John Prine's debut turned a Maywood, Illinois mail carrier into one of American songwriting's sharpest plain-spoken voices, pairing a heroin-addicted veteran in 'Sam Stone,' a strip-mined Kentucky town in 'Paradise,' and a lonely widow in 'Hello in There' with dry, funny-sad understatement. Arif Mardin's spare arrangements keep the focus on Prine's fingerpicked guitar and flat, conversational delivery. It is the field guide's start-here record for the whole country-folk storyteller lane and the direct model for deadpan songwriters from David Berman to MJ Lenderman.
lineage: Emerged from the same early-1970s Chicago folk-club scene as Steve Goodman, who discovered Prine and brought him to Kris Kristofferson's attention; directly seeded the deadpan funny-sad trunk line that runs through Bill Callahan and David Berman to MJ Lenderman.

label: Atlantic
description: Prine's second record leans further into bluegrass, cut fast and loose with brother Dave Prine on fiddle and a stripped-to-the-bone band. 'The Great Compromise' turns a drive-in-movie breakup into a Vietnam-era allegory about the country itself, while 'Souvenirs,' written with Steve Goodman, is one of Prine's plainest, saddest songs. The closing a cappella take on the Carter Family's title track ties the record straight back to the pre-1965 roots music this whole zone treats as source material.
lineage: Follows directly from John Prine (1971) and pulls its stripped-down string-band sound from the Carter Family and pre-bluegrass roots music that the Roots lane (R1) supplies to the whole atlas.

label: Atlantic
description: Recorded partly in Memphis with a rougher, more electric band, Sweet Revenge is Prine answering lukewarm reviews of his second album with sharper humor and a harder country edge. 'Christmas in Prison' turns an absurd premise into genuine tenderness, 'Please Don't Bury Me' is a rollicking, funny meditation on death and organ donation, and 'Dear Abby' mines an advice column for comic pathos. Critic Robert Christgau flagged the record as the one where cynicism became Prine's dominant voice.
lineage: Continues the storytelling style of the first two Atlantic albums while pulling Prine's sound closer to the honky-tonk and outlaw country of the neighboring V23 and V26 lanes.

label: Atlantic
description: Produced by Stax veteran Steve Cropper, Common Sense pushes Prine toward rock and R&B horns and is his most electric, produced record from the Atlantic years. 'Common Sense' and 'Come Back to Us Barbara Lewis Hare Krishna Beauregard' widen his storytelling into the drug culture and identity confusion of the mid-1970s. A closing cover of Chuck Berry's 'You Never Can Tell' underlines how much rock and roll sat underneath Prine's folk-country surface.
lineage: Marks Prine's furthest reach toward rock production before he moved to Asylum and pulled back toward the sparer sound of Bruised Orange.
key_tracks: Come Back to Us Barbara Lewis Hare Krishna Beauregard

label: Asylum
description: Produced by Steve Goodman after Prine had stalled out on an earlier, over-produced attempt, Bruised Orange is often called his most fully realized record: warm, plainspoken, and full of small-town detail. 'Fish and Whistle' and 'That's the Way That the World Goes 'Round' turn everyday disappointment into wry survival philosophy, while the title track processes a real childhood tragedy without ever raising its voice. It is the clearest bridge in Prine's catalog between funny and devastating, the quality the field guide calls the model for Lenderman-style humor.
lineage: Produced by fellow Chicago songwriter Steve Goodman, tying the two together as this lane's central Chicago-scene pairing, and it is the most-cited Prine album behind the deadpan funny-sad line that runs to David Berman and MJ Lenderman.
key_tracks: That's the Way That the World Goes 'Round

label: Asylum
description: Cut at Muscle Shoals Sound with producer Barry Beckett, Storm Windows closed out Prine's Asylum contract with a moodier, more country-soul-inflected sound than Bruised Orange. The title track and 'Living in the Future' keep his conversational storytelling intact while the arrangements lean on Southern session musicians. It is a lesser-known but well-regarded entry that fans of the deadpan storyteller sound often discover after the two records around it.
lineage: Closes the run of 1970s Atlantic and Asylum albums that established Prine's plainspoken template before his 1980s hiatus and 1984 return on his own Oh Boy label.

label: Oh Boy Records
description: Aimless Love was the first release on Prine's own Oh Boy Records, launched after major labels lost interest, and it set the independent, DIY model he kept for the rest of his career. 'Unwed Fathers,' written with Bobby Braddock, stands with 'Sam Stone' among his starkest character studies, while the loose, easy title track shows the funnier side of the same plainspoken voice. Shel Silverstein co-wrote the opener, tying two of this lane's storytellers directly together.
lineage: Begins the Oh Boy era of Prine's career, the self-released model later echoed by songwriters in the Drag City deadpan school (V2) and the modern barroom-storyteller lane (C2).

label: Oh Boy Records
description: Produced by Howie Epstein with guest turns from Tom Petty, Bruce Springsteen, and Bonnie Raitt, The Missing Years was Prine's commercial comeback after a mid-1980s lull and won him his first Grammy. The surreal title track imagines Jesus's unrecorded adolescence in the same dry, matter-of-fact voice Prine uses for barroom stories, and 'The Sins of Memphisto' is a widescreen character sketch of aging and regret. It proved the small-label, self-released model of Oh Boy Records could still reach a wide audience.
lineage: Reconnects 1990s roots-rock production with Prine's founding storytelling style, and is frequently cited by younger Oh Boy-adjacent songwriters as the album that brought him back into view.

label: Oh Boy Records
description: A covers album built around duets with Iris DeMent, Emmylou Harris, Lucinda Williams, and other women singers, In Spite of Ourselves has Prine largely stepping back from writing to interpret classic honky-tonk and country songs. The title track, one of only two Prine originals here, is a raunchy, tender list-song about a mismatched couple that became one of his most-loved later works. It shows the duet, classic-country side of the storyteller tradition this lane is built on.
lineage: Pulls the lane's storytelling style back toward its honky-tonk roots in V26, and the Iris DeMent duets in particular have been cited as a direct influence on 2010s husband-and-wife Americana duet acts.

label: Oh Boy Records
description: Prine's first album of new songs in nine years, Fair & Square is spare and unhurried, built mostly around acoustic guitar with light Nashville session backing. 'Clay Pigeons,' a Blaze Foley cover, and 'Some Humans Ain't Human' pair Prine's plainest philosophizing with his sharpest political jab of the era, aimed squarely at post-9/11 politics. It won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album and confirmed that Prine's understated storytelling had lost none of its force.
lineage: Represents the mature, unhurried version of the same plainspoken storytelling Prine established in 1971, still the reference point critics use decades later for MJ Lenderman-style humor.

label: Oh Boy Records
description: Prine's final album of new songs, produced by Dave Cobb, is a relaxed, plainly sung meditation on mortality that still finds room for jokes: 'When I Get to Heaven' imagines the afterlife as a party with a cocktail named after him. 'Summer's End' and 'The Lonesome Friends of Science' show the same unadorned character sketches he was writing in 1971, now aimed at old age instead of youth. The album debuted at No. 5 on the Billboard 200, proof that the deadpan storyteller lane he founded still had a wide audience.
lineage: Closes Prine's catalog on the same plainspoken storytelling that opened it, and its Dave Cobb production connects it to the 2010s Americana revival that includes many artists in the C2 and C5 lanes.

label: Mercury
description: Tom T. Hall's third album is a loose concept record about a Kentucky-born singer returning to his hometown, narrated in Hall's plain, conversational baritone. 'A Week in a Country Jail' and 'Shoeshine Man' are character sketches drawn from Hall's own pre-fame jobs and travels through rural Kentucky, and the title track sets the tone for the whole storyteller persona he built through the early 1970s. It is early evidence of the narrative songwriting that makes him the other central figure of this lane alongside Prine.
lineage: Establishes the small-town, first-person narrative style Hall carried through In Search of a Song and The Storyteller, directly paralleling the plainspoken songwriting Prine was developing in Chicago at the same time.
key_tracks: A Week in a Country Jail

album: Ballad of Forty Dollars and His Other Great Songs
label: Mercury
description: Named for the single that made Hall's name as a country hit songwriter, this album collects early narrative singles told from the point of view of ordinary working people, including a gravedigger owed money by the deceased he is burying. 'That's How I Got to Memphis,' written by Hall, became a standard later covered widely across country and Americana. It shows Hall working out the plainspoken, story-in-three-minutes formula he refined two years later on In Search of a Song.
lineage: Set the commercial template of narrative country singles that Hall expanded into full concept albums over the next several years, running parallel to Prine's own debut the same era.
key_tracks: That's How I Got to Memphis
I Washed My Face in the Morning Dew

label: Mercury
description: Hall wrote this album after driving through rural Kentucky collecting stories from the people he met, and later called it his own favorite record. 'The Year That Clayton Delaney Died' is a plain, moving elegy for a local guitar picker who shaped Hall's own musicianship, and 'Trip to Hyden' turns a mining-disaster news trip into understated reportage. Alongside John Prine's debut, it is the field guide's start-here record for the whole country-folk storyteller lane.
lineage: Hall's own favorite and most personal record, drawing directly on the Kentucky small-town material that defines the plainspoken narrative style shared with Prine, Goodman, and later Southern storytelling songwriters.
key_tracks: The Year That Clayton Delaney Died

label: Mercury
description: Written almost entirely by Hall, this album pairs the gentle hit 'Me and Jesus' with the satirical 'The Monkey That Became President,' a Watergate-era parable about political absurdity delivered in Hall's flat, wry storytelling voice. It shows the range of the storyteller persona: sincere gospel-tinged songs sitting next to pointed social commentary, all without raising its voice. The record reached the country top twenty and reinforced Hall's reputation as Nashville's most literate songwriter of the era.
lineage: Extends the narrative-song format of Ballad of Forty Dollars and In Search of a Song into topical and political territory, a move later echoed by storytelling songwriters in the Southern storytelling rock lane (V3).

label: Mercury
description: Released the same year as We All Got Together and..., The Storyteller leans into the nostalgic, first-person character sketches that earned Hall his nickname, none more so than '(Old Dogs, Children and) Watermelon Wine,' a barroom monologue about a janitor's plainspoken wisdom that became one of his signature hits. 'More About John Henry' extends his interest in American folk mythology, while the closing 'One More Song for Jesus' returns to the gospel side of his catalog. It is close to a mission statement for the whole storyteller persona.
lineage: Gave Hall the nickname The Storyteller and cemented the plain, first-person narrative approach that made him a direct peer of Prine within this lane.

album: Songs of Fox Hollow (For Children of All Ages)
label: Mercury
description: Named after Hall's Tennessee farm, this is a concept album of story-songs written for children but performed with the same plain, unpatronizing storytelling voice Hall used on his adult records. 'Sneaky Snake' became a novelty radio hit and remains his best-known song outside country-radio circles. It underlines how much of Hall's regular songwriting already worked like a fable, a trait that ties directly into the deadpan storytelling tradition this lane traces forward.
lineage: An outgrowth of the same plain, story-first songwriting Hall used on his adult albums, cited as an example of the storyteller approach carrying over into any subject matter.
key_tracks: The Mysterious Fox of the Hollow

label: Mercury
description: Mickey Newbury's second album is a moody concept record stitched together with recurring rain sound effects, turning a suite of heartbreak songs into something closer to a spoken-word tone poem than a conventional country record. 'She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye' and an early version of 'San Francisco Mabel Joy' show Newbury's hushed baritone and unhurried, almost cinematic phrasing. It became a quiet touchstone for the outlaw country songwriters who followed him in Nashville.
lineage: Newbury's Nashville circle overlapped directly with Kris Kristofferson and Waylon Jennings, feeding the outlaw country movement he helped inspire, while his mood-piece song construction anticipated the concept-album approach Lee Hazlewood was building on the West Coast at the same time.
key_tracks: She Even Woke Me Up to Say Goodbye

label: Elektra
description: 'Frisco Mabel Joy is Newbury's best-known album, built around 'An American Trilogy,' his medley of two Civil War-era songs and a spiritual that Elvis Presley later turned into a Las Vegas showstopper. The rest of the record keeps the same hushed, orchestrated melancholy, with 'How I Love Them Old Songs' and 'The Future's Not What It Used to Be' showing Newbury's gift for wistful, plainly sung reflection. It remains the most widely covered entry in his catalog.
lineage: Written within the same early-1970s Nashville songwriter circle as Kris Kristofferson and Tom T. Hall, and its orchestral, mood-first production directly influenced the countrypolitan wing of 1970s Nashville songwriting.
key_tracks: How I Love Them Old Songs
The Future's Not What It Used to Be

label: Elektra
description: Heaven Help the Child continues Newbury's run of hushed, orchestrated song cycles, built around the wrenching multi-generational title track and 'Cortelia Clark,' a haunting tribute to a blind street singer who died in a house fire. 'Why You Been Gone So Long' became one of Newbury's most recorded compositions in bluegrass circles, showing how his songs traveled even when his own recordings stayed under the radar. The record extends the tone-poem approach of Looks Like Rain into even bleaker territory.
lineage: Completes a run of early-1970s mood-piece albums that made Newbury one of Nashville's most respected songwriters' songwriters, a reputation that fed directly into the outlaw country movement around him.
key_tracks: Why You Been Gone So Long

label: Buddah Records
description: Steve Goodman's debut is anchored by 'City of New Orleans,' a train-travelogue song that Arlo Guthrie turned into a hit and that became one of the most-covered songs to come out of the Chicago folk scene. Goodman's light tenor and quick, conversational picking sit alongside two John Prine songs and the Goodman and Prine co-write 'You Never Even Call Me by My Name,' later a hit for David Allan Coe. It captures the tight, mutually supportive Chicago folk-club circuit that also produced Prine.
lineage: Goodman discovered and championed Prine in Chicago's Earl of Old Town folk club and brought him to Kris Kristofferson's attention, making the two artists' debut albums the twin foundation of this lane's Chicago wing.
key_tracks: You Never Even Call Me by My Name

label: Buddah Records
description: Goodman's second album widens his storytelling range, from Michael Smith's barroom-philosopher song 'The Dutchman' to 'The Ballad of Penny Evans,' a stark a cappella song sung from the point of view of a Vietnam war widow. Bob Dylan sat in on piano for the title track, a mark of how tightly connected the era's singer-songwriter circles were. It shows Goodman as a first-rate interpreter of other writers' songs as well as his own, a role he also played for Prine.
lineage: Grew from the same Chicago folk scene as Goodman's debut, and its blend of interpretation and original songwriting mirrors the way Prine and Goodman traded songs and stages throughout the early 1970s.

label: Asylum Records
description: Goodman's Asylum debut moves further from straight folk into good-humored eclecticism, mixing the fiddle-and-mandolin title tune with a John Prine cover, 'Blue Umbrella,' and 'Door Number Three,' co-written with Jimmy Buffett. It is looser and funnier than his earlier Buddah albums, closer to the freewheeling live shows that built Goodman's reputation as a performer. The record's mix of borrowed songs and originals again shows how tightly the Chicago folk circle around Prine and Goodman shared material.
lineage: Continues the collaborative Chicago-scene songwriting of Goodman's earlier records, this time pulling in Jimmy Buffett and reinforcing his role as an interpreter of Prine's songs.

label: Capitol Records
description: Bobbie Gentry wrote and helped arrange this Southern gothic concept record, built around the title track's famously unresolved mystery: why did Billie Joe McAllister jump off the Tallahatchie Bridge, and what did the narrator's family throw off it themselves. Gentry's low, unhurried alto and Jimmie Haskell's string arrangement turn small-town Delta gossip into something close to a short story. The single knocked the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's out of the top of the Billboard 200, an unusual pop breakthrough for a record this narratively dense.
lineage: Set a template for Southern gothic narrative songwriting that later Delta-set storytellers, including Prine's Kentucky material and the modern Southern storytelling rock lane, draw on.

label: Capitol Records
description: A loose concept album about a day in Delta country life, The Delta Sweete strings together Gentry originals and covers, including a mariachi-flavored 'Tobacco Road,' into a song cycle now treated as a lost classic of orchestrated Southern storytelling. 'Okolona River Bottom Band' opens with horns and strings over a swampy groove, while 'Reunion' turns a childhood jump-rope rhyme into a rhythmic vocal showcase. It sold poorly on release but has since been reissued and covered, including a 2011 tribute album by Mercury Rev and guests.
lineage: Deepens the Southern gothic, concept-album storytelling Gentry began on Ode to Billie Joe, and its song-cycle structure anticipates later Delta-set narrative records in the Southern storytelling rock lane.

label: Capitol Records
description: The title track of Fancy is Gentry's other signature story-song: a mother sells her daughter into prostitution as a last resort out of Louisiana poverty, and the daughter turns the situation into hard-won independence, a narrative later read as an early feminist country anthem. The rest of the record mixes Gentry originals with contemporary pop covers like James Taylor's 'Something in the Way He Moves,' showing her range as an interpreter as well as a writer. It earned her a Grammy nomination and remains her most covered song after 'Ode to Billie Joe.'
lineage: Extends the hard-luck Southern narrative songwriting of Gentry's earlier records into more explicitly political territory, a thread later picked up by Southern storytelling songwriters.
key_tracks: Something in the Way He Moves

label: Capitol Records
description: Gentry wrote, arranged, and produced every track on Patchwork, her most personal record and, as it turned out, her last studio album before she largely withdrew from recording. Critics at the time noted its strong autobiographical thread, and songs like 'Marigolds and Tangerines' and 'Beverly' continue the plainspoken, orchestrated storytelling of her earlier records without a single outside song. It stands as the quiet close of one of this lane's most distinctive songwriting careers.
lineage: Caps Gentry's run of self-written, self-produced concept records and is frequently cited as an overlooked forerunner of singer-songwriter-as-producer records that came later.

label: Mercury
description: A concept album about a fictional Western town, Trouble Is a Lonesome Town alternates Hazlewood's own deep, deadpan spoken narration between songs, making it one of the earliest full narrative concept records in country music. It predates this lane's main run by several years but establishes the storytelling-through-song-cycle approach Hazlewood carried into his 1970s LHI albums. His cavernous baritone and dry humor here are the direct blueprint for the noir character studies he later wrote for Nancy Sinatra and for his own Swedish-era records.
lineage: Predates and directly sets up Hazlewood's later concept albums, Cowboy in Sweden and Requiem for an Almost Lady, and its narrated-town format is an early forerunner of the storytelling techniques this whole lane is built around.
borderline_note: Released 1963, before this lane's stated 1967-1980 era, but kept as the direct model for Hazlewood's narrated concept-album storytelling that the assignment's seed list calls out explicitly.

label: LHI Records
description: Recorded as the soundtrack to a Swedish TV special after Hazlewood relocated to Stockholm, Cowboy in Sweden layers his cavernous baritone over lush, faintly psychedelic orchestration that AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine has called cinematic and druggy. 'No Train to Stockholm' and 'Leather and Lace,' a duet with Nina Lizell, keep the cowboy-outsider persona Hazlewood built with Nancy Sinatra but push the production further into orchestral pop. It is the strangest and most cultishly loved record of his LHI years.
lineage: Extends the noir concept-album approach of Trouble Is a Lonesome Town into fully orchestrated Cosmic American Music territory, later reissued and championed by Light in the Attic Records as a touchstone for 2000s cosmic-country revivalists.

label: Viking Records
description: A song cycle about the end of a relationship, Requiem for an Almost Lady is, in AllMusic critic Stanton Swihart's words, one of the most agonizing breakup records ever committed to tape, delivered entirely in Hazlewood's dry, world-weary baritone. Tracks like 'If It's Monday Morning' and 'L.A. Lady' move through anger, regret, and resignation in short, plainly titled vignettes rather than conventional verse-chorus songs. It shows the narrative concept-album format Hazlewood pioneered on Trouble Is a Lonesome Town applied to a single relationship instead of a whole town.
lineage: Continues the song-cycle storytelling format Hazlewood established a decade earlier, tightened into a single narrative arc, and reinforces his influence on later breakup-concept records across country and indie songwriting.

label: Viking Records
description: Recorded in Sweden, 13 is one of the odder entries in Hazlewood's catalog, built on heavy horn arrangements, thick basslines, and hard-hitting drums that push his usual narrated storytelling into something closer to orchestrated funk-pop. It never got a wide U.S. release at the time and has since become one of the rarer, more collectible titles in the Light in the Attic reissue campaign that revived interest in Hazlewood's 1970s work. It shows how far Hazlewood stretched the country-storyteller format once he was working outside the Nashville and Los Angeles industry systems.
lineage: Represents the furthest extension of the Swedish-era production experiments Hazlewood began on Cowboy in Sweden, keeping the storytelling persona while abandoning most conventional country instrumentation.

album: It's So Hard to Tell Who's Going to Love You the Best
label: Capitol Records
description: Karen Dalton recorded this debut reluctantly and reportedly never wanted it released, drawn largely from other writers' songs, including Fred Neil's 'Little Bit of Rain' and the blues standard 'It Hurts Me Too,' filtered through her cracked, elastic voice. She was a fixture of the same Greenwich Village folk clubs as Bob Dylan and Fred Neil but avoided the spotlight, making this one of the era's most private-feeling folk records. Its raw, largely solo arrangements sound closer to a field recording than a commercial folk release.
lineage: Emerged from the same early-1960s Greenwich Village folk scene as Dylan, Fred Neil, and Tim Hardin, several of whose songs she interprets here, and her phrasing has been cited as a direct influence on singers from Nick Cave to later indie-folk vocalists.
key_tracks: In the Evening (It's So Hard to Tell Who's Going to Love You the Best)

label: Just Sunshine Records
description: Dalton's second and final studio album is a more fully produced record than her debut, recorded at Bearsville Studios with a band that stretches her interpretations of songs by Paul Butterfield and the traditional 'Katie Cruel' into loose, soulful arrangements. Pitchfork's 9.0 reissue review called her an eccentric, intuitive interpreter who never wrote her own words but always sounded completely like herself. It has become the more widely heard of her two albums and a major reference point for the 2000s folk revival that reissued both records.
lineage: Recorded in the same Woodstock and Bearsville orbit as several other early-1970s singer-songwriters, and its rediscovery through Light in the Attic reissues has made Dalton a direct touchstone for 2000s and 2010s indie folk singers.
key_tracks: How Sweet It Is (To Be Loved by You)

label: Capitol Records
description: Fred Neil's self-titled album, later reissued as Everybody's Talkin', is considered his best by critic Richie Unterberger and a foundational record of the Greenwich Village folk scene, built on Neil's warm 12-string guitar and deep, unhurried baritone. 'The Dolphins' and 'Everybody's Talkin'' show his knack for plainspoken, image-driven songwriting that avoided the topical-protest mode common at the time; the latter became a hit for Harry Nilsson via the Midnight Cowboy soundtrack. It directly influenced the generation of singer-songwriters, including Dalton and Hardin, who built on his plain, unadorned storytelling style.
lineage: A foundational Greenwich Village folk record that Karen Dalton, Tim Hardin, and later country-folk storytellers drew on directly for its plain, image-based songwriting and warm baritone delivery.
key_tracks: I've Got a Secret (Didn't We Shake Sugaree)
borderline_note: Released 1966, just before this lane's 1967 start point, but kept as an explicitly seeded foundational record for the plainspoken folk-into-country storytelling style.

label: Capitol Records
description: A looser, more jam-oriented record than his debut, Sessions stretches several tracks past seven minutes, with Neil's guitar and voice floating over extended, largely improvised backing. 'Look Over Yonder' and 'Roll On Rosie' show Neil moving toward the loose, unhurried feel that would later define his Coconut Grove period, when he mostly retired from performing. It is a deep cut compared to his self-titled album but is valued by admirers for its patient, meditative version of his folk-baritone style.
lineage: Extends the plainspoken, unhurried songwriting of Neil's self-titled album into looser studio-jam territory, closing out his brief major-label recording career before he withdrew from the music industry.

label: Verve Forecast
description: Tim Hardin's debut is a spare, blues-inflected folk record built around his frail, aching voice and songs that read like short confessions rather than verse-chorus structures. 'Reason to Believe' and 'Misty Roses' became widely covered standards, the former a hit for Rod Stewart in 1971, even though Hardin's own version barely registered commercially. It is regarded as one of the most compelling folk-rock records of its era, and its plain, emotionally direct songwriting is a clear ancestor of the confessional storytelling this whole lane is built on.
lineage: Part of the same Greenwich Village folk circuit as Fred Neil and Karen Dalton, and Hardin's plain, confessional songwriting directly influenced Bobby Darin's pop covers as well as the singer-songwriter movement of the early 1970s.
borderline_note: Released 1966, just before this lane's 1967 start point, but kept as an explicitly seeded foundational Greenwich Village record.

label: Verve Forecast
description: Widely considered Hardin's best full album, Tim Hardin 2 is built around 'If I Were a Carpenter,' a plainspoken marriage proposal set to a simple, tender melody that Bobby Darin turned into a hit within months. Critic Richie Unterberger singles it out as the record where Hardin dropped his earlier blues leanings for a distinctive, string-tinged folk-rock voice. It cemented his reputation as a songwriter's songwriter even as his own career was already being undercut by heroin addiction.
lineage: Consolidates the confessional folk style of Hardin's debut, and through 'If I Were a Carpenter' became one of the most widely covered songs to come out of the Greenwich Village scene, feeding directly into mainstream pop and country repertoires.

label: Atlantic
description: Loudon Wainwright III's solo acoustic debut established him as one of the sharpest and funniest of the post-Dylan singer-songwriters, marketed briefly, and reluctantly on his part, as a new Dylan by Atlantic Records. The songs are unadorned confessionals and character studies delivered in a wry, sometimes cutting talk-singing style close to Prine's, though Wainwright's humor runs more self-lacerating than Prine's small-town empathy. It set up the confessional, comic songwriting he built a five-decade career on.
lineage: Emerged from the same early-1970s New York and Boston folk-club circuit that also produced Jesse Winchester and overlaps chronologically with Prine's funny-sad songwriting, though Wainwright's focus stays closer to his own family than to other characters.
key_tracks: Glad to See You've Got Religion

label: Atlantic
description: Album II keeps Wainwright's blunt, confessional style intact while sharpening the black comedy, from the seedy travelogue of 'Motel Blues' to the family satire of 'Nice Jewish Girls.' Recorded quickly in Boston with mostly solo acoustic arrangements, it shows Wainwright working the same plain, first-person storytelling territory as Prine but turned inward on his own bad behavior rather than outward onto other characters. It remains a favorite among fans for its rawer, funnier version of his confessional style.
lineage: Continues directly from Wainwright's debut, and its diaristic, self-mocking storytelling helped define the confessional-comic strain of 1970s singer-songwriting alongside Prine's more outward-looking character studies.
key_tracks: Saw Your Name in the Paper

label: Columbia
description: Wainwright's first record with a full backing band, billed as White Cloud, and his first for Columbia after leaving Atlantic, Album III is best known for the novelty hit 'Dead Skunk,' a jaunty singalong about roadkill that became his only Top 40 single. The rest of the record keeps his sharper, more personal songwriting intact, including a cover of Leiber and Stoller's 'Smokey Joe's Cafe,' showing he could still write and interpret plainspoken story-songs even while scoring a novelty hit. It marked the point where Wainwright's commercial visibility and his serious songwriting briefly lined up.
lineage: Its full-band arrangements and Columbia backing pulled Wainwright's plainspoken storytelling toward a more commercial folk-rock sound, distinguishing his catalog from the sparer Chicago-scene records of Prine and Goodman.

label: Columbia
description: Attempted Mustache pairs Wainwright's sharpest character songs yet, 'The Swimming Song' and 'The Man Who Couldn't Cry,' later covered by Johnny Cash, with looser, more eclectic material including a Woody Guthrie-derived closer inspired by a real 1970s guru's American tour. It shows Wainwright fully in command of the plainspoken, funny-sad storytelling voice he shares with Prine and Goodman, applied to his own increasingly complicated life rather than to outside characters. Critics still cite it as one of his most complete records of the decade.
lineage: Represents the commercial and creative high point of Wainwright's Columbia years and, through the Johnny Cash cover of 'The Man Who Couldn't Cry,' shows the same crossover into mainstream country storytelling that Prine's songs achieved through other artists.
key_tracks: I Am the Way (New York Town)

label: Ampex Records
description: Memphis-born Jesse Winchester moved to Montreal in 1967 to avoid the Vietnam draft, and his debut, produced by Robbie Robertson of the Band, channels that homesick distance directly into plainspoken songs about the American South he could no longer visit. 'The Brand New Tennessee Waltz' and 'Yankee Lady' pair warm, unhurried melodies with a quiet ache that critics have compared to the Band's own rootsy storytelling. Because he could not tour the United States for years, the album built its reputation almost entirely on word of mouth among other songwriters.
lineage: Produced by Robbie Robertson and steeped in the same rootsy, plainspoken songwriting the Band was developing at the same time, directly linking Winchester's exile narratives to the Dylan and the Band lineage (V22) this whole zone traces back to.

label: Bearsville
description: Winchester's second album continues the plainspoken, homesick songwriting of his debut with a slightly fuller, more soulful sound, still built around his warm, unhurried voice. Critic Robert Christgau praised its craft while noting Winchester's narrow emotional range, a fair description of a record that stays close to gentle regret and small, specific memories rather than drama. It reinforced Winchester's reputation among other songwriters even though, unable to tour the United States, he remained a cult figure rather than a star.
lineage: Follows directly from Winchester's debut, keeping the exile-songwriter perspective that ties him to the same Band-adjacent roots-rock lineage running through this lane.

label: Bearsville
description: By 1977, with a Vietnam-era amnesty finally letting him perform in the United States again, Winchester made his most fully realized album, featuring guest turns from Emmylou Harris and James Burton and a loping title track that became a minor FM-radio favorite. 'Rhumba Man' and 'Bowling Green' show him writing with a lighter, more optimistic touch than his exile-era records, without losing the plainspoken clarity of his debut. Rate Your Music's own listeners tag the album simply as country folk, a fair summary of Winchester's whole catalog.
lineage: Marks Winchester's return to U.S. visibility after years of exile in Montreal, and its warmer, more collaborative sound, aided by Nashville and Muscle Shoals session players, closes the arc that began with his Band-adjacent debut.

label: Columbia
description: Eric Andersen's highest-charting album, Blue River pairs his plainspoken, romantic songwriting with a warm, string-inflected folk-rock production that drew comparisons to Carole King and James Taylor. Joni Mitchell sings uncredited harmony on the title track, and 'Is It Really Love at All' shows Andersen's move from his earlier topical folk toward the intimate, relationship-focused songwriting that dominates the record. A master-tape mishap kept Andersen from following it up for years, but Blue River remains the album most critics point to as his best.
lineage: Moved Andersen's songwriting away from the topical Greenwich Village folk of his Vanguard years toward the plainer, more personal storytelling shared with Newbury and Jesse Winchester in the same period.
key_tracks: Is It Really Love at All

album: Boy Named Sue (And His Other Country Songs)
label: RCA Victor
description: Best known as a cartoonist and children's author, Shel Silverstein was also a prolific country songwriter, and this album collects his own versions of comic story-songs including 'A Boy Named Sue,' which Johnny Cash turned into a live hit at San Quentin the same year. Produced by Chet Atkins and Felton Jarvis in Nashville, the record leans on the same absurdist, punchline-driven storytelling that made Silverstein's poetry famous, just set to honky-tonk arrangements. It shows how directly the country-storyteller tradition of this lane overlapped with novelty and comedy songwriting.
lineage: Silverstein's Nashville songwriting connections to Johnny Cash and Bobby Bare tie him directly into the outlaw and mainstream country worlds this lane borders, and his comic, plainspoken storytelling is a direct precursor to the funny-sad tradition Prine and Goodman built up at the same time.

label: Columbia
description: Freakin' at the Freakers Ball moves Silverstein's comic storytelling from Nashville country parody into early-1970s counterculture satire, skewering drug culture, sex, and hippie pretension with the same singsong bluntness he used in his poetry. 'Sarah Cynthia Sylvia Stout Would Not Take the Garbage Out' later became one of his most famous published poems, showing how directly his song lyrics and children's verse fed each other. Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show, who Silverstein wrote extensively for, later covered the title track, tying this record into the same wry storytelling lineage as Prine and Goodman's Chicago scene.
lineage: Silverstein's dual career as a cartoonist and Nashville country songwriter made him a direct bridge between comic storytelling and country songcraft, an influence later cited by deadpan songwriters in the Prine lineage.
key_tracks: I Got Stoned and I Missed It

label: White Whale Records
description: Jim Ford's only album released in his lifetime blends country storytelling with deep soul and funk, recorded in Los Angeles with a band that included Elvis guitarist James Burton and organist Dr. John, and named for the Kentucky county where Ford was born. It is filled with unassuming, midtempo rockers and ballads about love and driving, a plainspoken, groove-driven cousin to the more acoustic storytelling elsewhere in this lane. Ford wrote songs later covered by Aretha Franklin, Bobby Womack, and Nick Lowe, but this record sold poorly and he drifted out of the industry soon after.
lineage: Ford's country-soul songwriting fed directly into other artists' hits, including Aretha Franklin's 'Niki Hoeky' and Bobby Womack's catalog, even as his own recording career stalled, and Harlan County has since been reclaimed by reissue labels as a missing link between Southern storytelling and Muscle Shoals-style country soul.
key_tracks: I Wanna Make Her Love Me
